core: Working definition of fieldwork: firsthand study of people in their own settings, living among them for months or years
Why fieldwork matters: books and secondhand accounts cannot substitute for presence
The fieldwork process: choose a site, build relationships, observe, record, analyze, write
Fieldwork methods: interviews, surveys, mapping, archival work
Honest note: the fieldworker is the instrument
Honest framing: fieldwork as anthropology's rite of passage
supporting: Armchair anthropology and why it failed
Malinowski's Trobriand Islands fieldwork and the professionalization of ethnography
Ethnography as the written product of fieldwork
outOfScope: Fieldwork ethics, consent, and IRB protocols (sibling topic: anthropology:foundations:fieldwork-ethics)
Survey research design and sampling (owned by the sociology subject)
Biographical detail on individual anthropologists beyond one-line attributions

claims.claim: Fieldwork is the firsthand study of people in their own settings: the working definition, from OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology, is a research method that requires cultural anthropologists to live for many months or years in the societies they study, adopting local ways of living, eating, dressing, and speaking as closely as possible.
Fieldwork is one of the most important practices of anthropology, and every subfield of anthropology conducts fieldwork in some form, though methods differ by subfield.

The establishment of ethnography as a professional field is identified with Bronisław Malinowski's fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands of Melanesia (c. 1915) and Margaret Mead's first fieldwork in Samoa (1925).

Nineteenth-century armchair anthropology built theories about human societies from secondhand materials — accounts by traders, missionaries, and colonial administrators — rather than from firsthand research, and such accounts were often unreliable because outsiders misunderstood what they saw or had interests that colored their reports.

Malinowski's Trobriand fieldwork involved living in a tent among the people, speaking the local language fluently, recording interviews and observations on the scene; his private diaries frankly recorded the isolation and strain of field life.
Malinowski published the results of his Trobriand research as Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922).

Fieldwork methods include interviews (researchers asking questions of informants chosen for their insider knowledge), survey questions posed to many people, mapping (documenting where things happen), and archival work with documents and records; fieldworkers keep records such as notebooks, computer files, recordings, photographs, and film.

Fieldwork is demanding: researchers often feel out of place on arrival in unfamiliar settings, typically need to learn a local language or dialect, and must negotiate access to the community they study.

Ethnography is shaped by the personal background and identity of the researcher — the fieldworker is the instrument — and earlier anthropologists' assumption that long-term intensive fieldwork alone guaranteed cross-cultural insight is now treated as a mistake.
Ethnographic fieldwork has become a sort of rite of passage into the profession of cultural anthropology.

Fieldwork is often described in almost heroic terms, while researchers' own accounts emphasize prosaic beginnings, awkward first days, and lessons learned through relationships and participation in ordinary life.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Heroic versus mundane portrayals of fieldwork
positions: Fieldwork is frequently narrated as a heroic journey of discovery (SAPIENS notes this framing is common).

Practitioners describe prosaic, awkward, and strained beginnings: Cohen's first lesson in Oaxaca was an early-morning summons to a wedding where he had to learn the rules of gift-giving on the spot; Malinowski's private diaries recorded isolation and frustration.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both sides honestly: fieldwork is a demanding, transforming practice (the rite of passage), and the transformation is rarely glamorous — the heroic image and the human reality coexisted from the discipline's founding.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does long-term fieldwork alone produce an insider's point of view?
positions: Earlier anthropologists believed that long-term intensive fieldwork was enough to give them insight into the perspectives of the people they studied.
Contemporary anthropology holds that ethnography is shaped by the researcher's own background and identity, and emphasizes collaboration with the community as a corrective.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches that presence is necessary but not automatic: the fieldworker is the instrument, so honest fieldwork acknowledges positionality and depends on relationships rather than assuming neutrality.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Anthropology: Chapter 1 Key Terms (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture (2022-10-05) of the canonical OpenStax URL; openstax.org blocks direct fetch. Source of the working definition of fieldwork used in the lesson: a research method requiring cultural anthropologists to live for many months or years in the societies they study, adopting local ways of living, eating, dressing, and speaking as closely as possible. Also defines armchair anthropology and interview.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Anthropology: Chapter 2 Introduction, Methods: Cultural and Archaeological (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture (2022-09-30) of the canonical OpenStax URL. Supports: fieldwork is one of the most important practices of anthropology; all subfields conduct fieldwork in some form; the concept of 'the field' was traditionally based on traveling to distant regions.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Anthropology: 2.3 Ethnography and Ethnology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture (2022-09-24) of the canonical OpenStax URL. Supports: ethnography as the method of creating a description of a culture; armchair anthropology as theory based solely on secondhand information; the challenge of observing without bias.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Anthropology: 2.4 Participant Observation and Interviewing (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture (2022-10-07) of the canonical OpenStax URL. Supports: researchers' discomfort on arrival in unfamiliar settings; record-keeping (field notebooks, computer files, recordings, photographs, film); interviews with informants chosen for insider knowledge; survey questions as an additional tool; long-term trusting relationships. Participant-observation technique itself is covered by the sibling topic and is not developed here.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Anthropology: 2.5 Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture (2022-10-06) of the canonical OpenStax URL. sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Anthropology: 1.7 Reaching for an Insider's Point of View (OpenStax)

sourceRecords.title: The Uninvited Invitados (SAPIENS)
sourceRecords.notes: Fetched live 2026-08-22 (sapiens.org reachable). Essay by anthropologist Jeffrey H. Cohen about his first fieldwork in Santa Ana del Valle, Oaxaca, Mexico. Supports the honest framing: fieldwork is 'often described in terms that can seem almost heroic,' while real beginnings are prosaic — an early-morning summons, a wedding as a first lesson, learning local rules of reciprocity through a gift book. Used as evidence for the honest note; summarized in original prose, no wording reproduced.
